http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27920.text: Big News Network.com Trumps war on far-left terrorism goes global A landmark meeting in Washington put far-left extremism at the center of international counterterrorism efforts For years, liberal elites across the West dismissed warnings about far-left extremism as relics of the Cold War or right-wing paranoia. Today, the evidence is undeniable. A recent US-led global initiative has the ambition to finally confront this resurgence of political terrorism with the seriousness it demands. This is not a partisan crusade but a defense of civilization against those who would burn it down in the name of utopia. The West in flames Europe is bleeding from a thousand cuts inflicted by far-left networks. Railways have been repeatedly sabotaged, power grids targeted, and commercial enterprises struck, inflicting billions in cumulative losses while paralyzing supply chains and public services. Police officers have been assaulted, elected officials threatened, and communities shaken - echoing the days of the 1970s Red Brigades and Baader-Meinhof. In Germany, far-left violence surged more than 40% in a single year. The authorities logged 321 sabotage investigations in 2025 alone, which were overwhelmingly aimed at military, police, railway, and energy targets. Climate activism has fused with anti-capitalism, class warfare, feminism, and outright hostility to European industry and traditional values. What begins as protests and occupations too often escalates to sabotage harming ordinary citizens. The longest blackout in Berlin since World War II struck in early 2026, courtesy of the Vulkangruppe (Volcano Group). This far-left outfit, active since 2011 with at least 13 attacks under its belt, torched power cables near a gas-fired plant, plunging tens of thousands of households and businesses into darkness for days amid freezing temperatures. Hospitals switched to emergency power, trains halted, and daily life fractured. Their manifesto framed it as "resistance" against fossil fuels and capitalism, but the victims were everyday Germans. Italy tells a similar story of escalating chaos. During the Winter Olympics, coordinated rail sabotages forced the cancellation of roughly 40,000 train services. A premature explosion later killed two anarchists preparing yet another railway assault. Official figures show a staggering 450% rise in anti-train sabotages in 2024-2025. An attack on the TAL oil pipeline left it offline for five days. In Greece, over 80% of radical violence stems from far-left actors. These attacks are not isolated incidents but manifestations of a broader pattern of escalating political violence. In the US, violent far-left actors accounted for 63% of recorded anti-government attacks and plots in 2025. Their tactics have expanded beyond sabotage to include targeted political assassinations, including the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The threat is transnational, fluid, and growing bolder. The networks and their enablers Behind the violence lies a web of organizations blending climate hysteria with revolutionary ideology. Groups like Antifa, operating across borders, exemplify the danger. The US has designated four violent far-left entities from Germany, Italy, and Greece as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. Hungary under Viktor Orban took similar action after Antifa thugs attacked a peaceful patriotic march in Budapest, injuring participants. A 2025 European Parliament motion, backed by dozens of MEPs, called for declaring Antifa a terrorist organization and investigating its financial ties - including potential links to George Soros. Support from certain foundations - such as those associated with Soros or Germany's Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung - has sustained overlapping causes that blend radical left objectives with broader progressive efforts. Mainstream media and the liberal establishment obsessively spotlight far-right threats - often conflating them with patriotic or conservative voices - while downplaying or excusing far-left excesses. In parts of the EU, these networks have infiltrated state administrations and influential think tanks, embedding ideology into governance. This funding ecosystem sustains a global far-left apparatus that exploits open borders, lenient justice systems, and elite guilt to advance its aims. Ongoing legal proceedings, such as those in Dresden involving serious charges against Antifa members, underscore the organized nature of the threat. Trump's America steps up The Trump administration has unleashed a global campaign to crush this radical left terrorism. In mid-July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism in Washington, drawing representatives from over 65 countries, including participants from Europe, Latin America, Africa, and Asia, to address this shared challenge to governance, infrastructure security, and citizen safety. The ministerial yielded concrete outcomes that mark a new phase of coordinated international action. Delegates forged agreement on three hard-hitting pillars of action: ramped-up designations and accountability, with the US already branding four dangerous far-left groups as terrorists and reviewing more; deeper operational teamwork through intensified intelligence sharing, coordinated travel bans, and urgent defenses for railways, power grids, and other critical lifelines; and fresh US visa restrictions slamming the door on those who engage in or bankroll far-left terror. Germany stepped forward to host the next working session, while Treasury officials vowed to tear apart funding pipelines with rewards of up to millions for tips that disrupt the money flow. The approach closes critical gaps in global counterterrorism frameworks. The US is now treating far-left extremism with the same ferocity once reserved for jihadists: designating groups, imposing sanctions and visa restrictions, disrupting finances, and fostering international cooperation. Importantly, the campaign zeroes in on extremist organizations rather than any particular government or geopolitical rival. This fight against a shared ideological enemy - one hostile to traditional societies, national identities, and ordered liberty - offers common ground. Powers such as China and Russia, with their own experiences managing ideological extremism and emphasis on domestic order, might stand to benefit from - and contribute to - practical cooperation in safeguarding stability and development. The cost of selective silence The liberal establishment's selective outrage is damning. While far-right actors - frequently defenders of national sovereignty and cultural continuity - face relentless scrutiny and persecution, far-left violence is often romanticized as "protest" or explained away as a reaction to "injustice." This double standard has emboldened extremists, allowing them to infiltrate institutions and erode public safety. The US initiative may mark a turning point, both for Western countries and beyond. By placing violent far-left networks within a broader counterterrorism framework, strengthening investigations, disrupting financial support, and expanding international cooperation, it advances the principle that no movement is exempt from accountability when it embraces violence. Other governments can contribute by improving intelligence sharing, addressing transnational networks, and ensuring that public safety remains above political considerations. As violent far-left extremism becomes increasingly transnational, governments cannot afford selective approaches to political violence. Attacks on critical infrastructure and politically motivated violence threaten security, economic resilience, and public confidence across regions. A broad international coalition focused on confronting violent extremism can help reinforce a fundamental principle: political grievances cannot be pursued through terror. https://www.politico.eu/article/afd-alte.text: STRASBOURG — The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) wants to scrap the directly elected European Parliament, shrink the European Commission and let Berlin opt out of common EU policies. That’s according to the party’s policy program, which party leader Alice Weidel will present at the European Parliament on Wednesday. The AfD’s push comes as far-right parties look to gain ground across Europe. The party’s recent victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have given it fresh momentum. Last week, Marine Le Pen was in Brussels to outline her plan for the EU if she becomes French president. She vowed to halve Paris’ contributions to the budget if she gets to power, and to turn the European Commission into a “secretariat” in the service of its member countries. Advertisement Advertisement “I’m not fooled by what the European Commission wants to do. The European Commission wants to turn itself into a state; we do not. And so we will stand in its way,” Le Pen said. The AfD policy paper, obtained by Brussels Playbook , says the AfD would not seek to leave the EU or eurozone at first. Instead, it wants to renegotiate the EU treaties and cut the bloc’s powers, institutions and budget. Weidel will present her strategy at an event on Wednesday afternoon entitled “Our new deal for Europe.” The party wants to replace direct European Parliament elections with delegates appointed by national parliaments, reduce the Commission’s role to purely administrative and transfer decision-making to national capitals. It also wants to replace the EU’s top court with an arbitration tribunal. The plan calls for slashing and capping the EU budget, freezing staffing numbers and abolishing agencies. The AfD would use its veto power to scrap revenue from VAT and plastics taxes, and threaten to halt Berlin’s contributions to the common budget to force through the reforms it demands. “If Brussels refuses the path of reform, this veto will be used to block future EU financing legislation and drastically reduce Germany’s contributions,” the AfD plan says. The AfD also wants to give larger eurozone economies more voting power at the European Central Bank — giving Germany a say in monetary policy — and reject the digital euro. Advertisement Advertisement Berlin should seek exemptions from EU rules on migration, taxation, social policy, defense and common borrowing, the party argues. If the EU’s green policies are not scrapped, and no substantial changes take place to industrial, agriculture, and financial policies, an opt out in these areas would be sought too. The paper identifies 2029 — when the next European Parliament and German federal elections will take place — as the moment to start implementing the reforms. “In 2029, something we have scarcely dared to hope for may become reality: a patriotic, right-wing majority in the European Parliament is coming within reach.” If its reforms fail, the AfD says it would put Germany’s EU membership to a referendum.

https://www.dw.com/en/police-in-northern.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HjDK Details of the incident, including the number of suspects or motive, were initially unclear Image: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement A BMW was driven ​deliberately ‌into a group of people, leaving ‌four to five of ‌them ​with some serious but not life-threatening injuries in Neustadt am Rübenberge late on Monday night, police said on Tuesday morning. A police patrol making routine traffic checks in town near Hannover in the state of Lower Saxony, intervened, shooting at the car to stop it. "The officers witnessed the incident as it happened and opened fire on the vehicle after it had been driven into the group of people," the spokesperson said. Organized crime suspected Police announced that they had taken three people into custody at the BMW owner's address. A police spokesperson added that initial findings indicated the ramming was an act of gang violence between organized crime families, that the individuals involved knew each other and that the perpetrators likely targeted the group of people and were not acting at random. Forensic analysis of the crime scene was ongoing, a police spokesperson said Image: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance Several suspects had fled the scene of the ramming on foot, police had said. "The sequence of events and the exact roles of those involved are still under investigation," the spokesperson said, adding that forensic analysis of the cars and ramming scene was ongoing. A reporter for the German DPA news agency described several damaged cars, with flat tires, a smashed rear window and bullet holes.
